lead: This unit shows how a raw sensor voltage becomes a number on a screen or a motion at a shaft. You will learn signal conditioning, data acquisition, the bridges that measure unknown components, the amplifiers and displays of a measuring chain, and the pneumatic, electrical and micro actuators that drive real loads, from a press to a syringe pump. After it you can size an amplifier and filter, choose a sampling rate, balance a bridge, read a DVM or a DSO, and pick the right actuator for a job.
about: The unit runs from the sensor to the load. It starts by conditioning the raw signal (amplify, filter, linearise, isolate), collects those signals into a data acquisition system with a known resolution and sampling rate, and carries them from plant to control room. The output side follows: pneumatic and hydraulic power, solenoids, relays and motors, steppers and servos, and micro actuators. It then returns to the measurement front end with the DC and AC bridges used for resistance, inductance and capacitance, goes deeper into filters, pre-amplifiers, differential and isolation amplifiers, and ends at the display: DVM, multimeter, CRO, DSO and spectrum analyser.

chapters.idea: Signal conditioning turns a weak, noisy, non-linear sensor output into a clean standard voltage or current that the next stage can digitise safely.
chapters.depth: Cover the four jobs in the order they usually appear: amplification (gain, offset, instrumentation amplifier), filtering (a first-order RC low-pass with fc = 1/(2πRC) to kill mains hum and switching noise), linearisation (breakpoint circuits and software lookup tables for thermocouples and thermistors) and electrical isolation (transformer and opto-coupler, breaking ground loops, surge protection). Add attenuation for large signals and impedance matching so a high-source-impedance sensor is not loaded. Some syllabi call the whole chain 'signal conditioning and processing'. Keep every formula at first-order level.

figure.title: Signal conditioning chain
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain from a 2 mV sensor through a gain-500 amplifier, a 16 Hz low-pass filter, a lineariser and an isolator to a 0-5 V output.

chapters.example: A strain gauge bridge gives 2 mV at full load. A difference amplifier has Rf = 100 kΩ and Rin = 200 Ω, so gain = Rf/Rin = 500 and the output is 2 mV × 500 = 1 V. A low-pass filter with R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 µF has fc = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶) = 15.9 Hz. Find the gain, the amplifier output and the filter cutoff.
chapters.trap: Gain multiplies the offset drift and the noise along with the signal, so a large gain alone does not improve accuracy. Also keep gain in dB (20 log₁₀ of the voltage ratio) separate from plain voltage ratio.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (sensitivity, linearity, accuracy) and Unit 2 (strain gauge bridge output).
chapters.leave: ADC conversion and sampling theory to 6.2; filter families and op-amp internal design to 6.9.

chapters.idea: A data acquisition system converts many analogue sensor signals into digital numbers with known resolution, sampling rate and channel order.
chapters.depth: Name and order the elements: transducer, signal conditioning, multiplexer, sample-and-hold, ADC, controller and memory, display or bus. Resolution in volts = full-scale span / 2ⁿ for an n-bit ADC. Give the sampling rule: the highest signal frequency must stay below half the sampling rate, and per-channel rate = total converter rate / number of channels scanned. Mention sample-and-hold aperture time and why it matters when the input moves during conversion. List converter types by name only: successive approximation, flash, sigma-delta. Mention PC plug-in card, stand-alone and distributed/SCADA architectures in one line each.

figure.title: Elements of a DAS
figure.aria: A left-to-right block chain: transducer, conditioner, 8-channel multiplexer scanning 4 channels, sample-and-hold, 12-bit ADC taking 250 microseconds, processor, then store and display.

chapters.example: A DAS has 8 input channels, an input range of ±5 V, a 12-bit ADC, and scans 4 channels at 1 kS/s each. Span = 10 V, so resolution = 10 V / 4096 = 2.44 mV. Total converter rate = 4 × 1000 = 4000 samples/s, so each conversion must finish in 1/4000 = 250 µs. The highest signal frequency allowed per channel is 1000/2 = 500 Hz. Find resolution, conversion time and maximum signal frequency.
chapters.trap: Students apply the half-sampling-rate rule to each channel while forgetting that one shared ADC divides its speed among all scanned channels; the per-channel rate is total rate divided by channel count.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for signal conditioning; Unit 1 dynamic characteristics for response time.
chapters.leave: Converter internal circuits; detailed sampling and aliasing mathematics to 6.10.

chapters.idea: Signal transmission carries a measurement from the sensor to the readout without picking up noise, losing accuracy or creating ground errors.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Keep it short. Cover the 2-wire 4-20 mA current loop: live zero at 4 mA, current is independent of wire resistance, loop resistance limit from the supply voltage, sense resistor converts current to voltage. Compare with voltage transmission over long cable. Mention screened twisted pair, 3-wire RTD and 4-wire resistance connection to cancel lead resistance. Name RS-485, HART and fieldbus as digital options, and fibre or wireless in one line each.

figure.title: Two-wire current loop
figure.aria: A sensor feeding a 4-20 mA transmitter, a loop cable of up to 700 ohms total, a 250 ohm sense resistor giving 1-5 V, and the receiver ADC.

chapters.example: A 2-wire transmitter runs from a 24 V supply and needs 10 V across itself. The receiver uses a 250 Ω sense resistor. Maximum loop resistance = (24 − 10) / 0.020 = 700 Ω. At 4 mA the sense voltage is 4 mA × 250 Ω = 1 V; at 20 mA it is 20 mA × 250 Ω = 5 V. Find the loop resistance limit and the receiver voltage range.
chapters.trap: In a live-zero loop, 0 mA means a broken wire or dead transmitter, not a zero reading. Treat it as a fault, not as a measurement.
chapters.leave: Digital bus protocols and network layers; fibre optic sensor physics to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Pneumatic and hydraulic actuators use pressure in air or oil to produce large force and motion with simple, robust, spark-free hardware.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Pneumatics: compressor at about 6-8 bar, FRL unit (filter, regulator, lubricator), direction control valve such as a 5/2 solenoid valve, single-acting and double-acting cylinders, force F = pA, speed set by flow control. Hydraulics: oil at 100-200 bar, relief valve, servo valve, much higher force and stiffness. Electro-pneumatic actuator: solenoid valve switched by an electrical signal. Selection criteria: force needed, stroke, speed, stiffness, cleanliness, noise, cost per unit force.

figure.title: Pneumatic actuation chain
figure.aria: Compressed air at 6 bar passing through a filter-regulator-lubricator unit and a 5/2 solenoid valve into a 50 mm bore cylinder that pushes a 1060 N load.

chapters.example: A double-acting cylinder has bore 50 mm and runs on air at 6 bar gauge with a mechanical efficiency of 0.9. Piston area = π/4 × (0.050)² = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m². Theoretical force = 6 × 10⁵ Pa × 1.963 × 10⁻³ m² = 1178 N. Usable force = 1178 × 0.9 = 1060 N. Find the extension force.
chapters.trap: Extension and retraction forces differ because the rod removes area on the rod side; and pressure given in bar is gauge pressure, not absolute.
chapters.prereq: None beyond basic force and pressure from school physics.
chapters.leave: Solenoid coil operation to 6.5; micro-scale fluidic actuation to 6.7.

chapters.idea: Electrical actuators turn current into motion: a solenoid gives a short linear stroke, a relay switches contacts, and a motor gives continuous rotation.
chapters.depth: Solenoid: coil, plunger, force-stroke curve, pull-in and hold current, duty cycle and heating. Relay: coil voltage and power, armature, normally open and normally closed contacts, contact current and voltage rating separate from coil rating, solid-state relay using a triac or back-to-back thyristors. DC motor: back emf Eb = V − IaRa, torque proportional to armature current, speed roughly proportional to applied voltage, shunt, series and permanent-magnet types. AC motor: three-phase induction motor, slip, synchronous motor. Give speed-torque characteristics and name the high starting current of induction motors.

figure.aria: A hierarchy splitting electrical actuators into solenoid for short linear stroke, relay for switching contacts, and motor for rotation, with motor split into DC and AC induction.

chapters.example: A permanent-magnet DC motor runs from 12 V and draws 2 A at full load. Armature resistance is 1 Ω. Input power = 12 × 2 = 24 W. Back emf Eb = 12 − (2 × 1) = 10 V. If the shaft output is 18 W, efficiency = 18/24 = 0.75, that is 75%. Find back emf and efficiency.
chapters.trap: A relay has two separate ratings, coil voltage and contact rating; a 24 V coil says nothing about the 230 V mains it may switch. Also do not ignore motor starting current, which can be several times the full-load value.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (magnetic circuits, inductance) for coil behaviour.
chapters.leave: Stepper and servo closed-loop control to 6.6; piezo and electrostatic micro actuation to 6.7.

chapters.idea: A stepper motor moves in fixed angular steps counted open-loop, while a servo motor uses feedback to hold a commanded position or speed.
chapters.depth: Stepper: step angle = 360° / steps per revolution; variable-reluctance, permanent-magnet and hybrid types; full-step, half-step and microstepping; phase energisation sequence; pull-in and pull-out torque; maximum stepping rate; resonance. Servo: error signal from a potentiometer or encoder, closed-loop correction, DC servo and AC servo with resolver, position, speed and torque modes. Compare open-loop stepping (cheap, may lose steps) with closed-loop servo (accurate, stable, costlier). Speed and position calculations with a lead screw.

figure.aria: A four-step timing chart in which phases A, B, A-bar and B-bar are energised one after another, one step each.

chapters.example: A stepper motor has a step angle of 1.8°, so steps per revolution = 360/1.8 = 200. It is driven by 1000 pulses per second. Speed = 1000/200 = 5 rev/s = 300 rpm. The shaft drives a lead screw of pitch 5 mm, so linear speed = 5 rev/s × 5 mm = 25 mm/s. Find the step rate, the speed and the table speed.
chapters.trap: Step angle is the mechanical step, not the final resolution once microstepping is used, and available torque falls sharply as stepping rate rises; a motor that starts under load may stall when accelerated.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.5 for motor principle and back emf.
chapters.leave: Motor magnetic design and drive electronics detail.

chapters.idea: Micro actuators make small motions by electrostatic attraction, piezoelectric strain or shape-memory phase change, because coils and magnets do not shrink well.
chapters.depth: Piezoelectric: inverse piezo effect, charge-to-strain, d33 coefficient, strain around 0.1%, high force and stiffness, small stroke, kHz response, stack and bimorph bending types, applications in inkjet heads, micropumps and autofocus. Shape memory alloy: thermal phase change, 4-8% recoverable strain, slow cooling, large hysteresis. Electrostatic: parallel-plate and comb drive, force proportional to V², pull-in instability at one-third of the gap, needs tens of volts. Magnetic micro actuation and fluidic actuation in a line each as other principles. Applications: RF MEMS switch, accelerometer, micro mirror.

figure.aria: Three families of micro actuator under one root: piezoelectric with 0.1 percent strain, shape memory alloy with 4 to 8 percent strain and slow response, and electrostatic with pull-in at one third of the gap.

chapters.example: A parallel-plate electrostatic actuator has a square plate 200 µm × 200 µm, a gap of 2 µm and an applied voltage of 30 V. Take ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. Area = 4 × 10⁻⁸ m². Capacitance = ε0A/g = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 4 × 10⁻⁸ / 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.177 pF. Force = ε0AV²/(2g²) = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 4 × 10⁻⁸ × 900 / (2 × 4 × 10⁻¹²) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ N, about 40 µN. Pull-in occurs when the gap falls to g/3 = 0.67 µm. Find capacitance, force and the pull-in gap.
chapters.trap: Ignoring pull-in: beyond one-third of the initial gap the electrostatic force grows faster than the restoring spring force, the plates snap together and a simple voltage control cannot hold intermediate positions.
chapters.leave: Fabrication and comb-drive design detail to Unit 5; macro fluid power to 6.4.

chapters.idea: A bridge finds an unknown resistance, inductance or capacitance by balancing it against known components until the detector reads zero.
chapters.depth: Wheatstone bridge: four arms, balance condition R1/R2 = R3/R4, null detector, sensitivity and the poor performance at very low resistance. Kelvin double bridge: four-terminal connection with ratio arms, cancels lead and contact resistance for values below about 1 Ω. Maxwell bridge: measures inductance with Q from about 1 to 10, balance gives L = R2R3C1. Hay bridge: for high Q above 10, series RC arm. Schering bridge: measures capacitance and dissipation factor tan δ at high voltage. Draw the bridge, derive or state the balance equation, and say which bridge suits which component and range.

figure.aria: A diamond bridge with source nodes A and D, ratio nodes B and C, four impedance arms Z1 to Z4, and a dashed detector branch between B and C.

chapters.example: A Wheatstone bridge has R1 = 100 Ω in the first arm, R2 = 200 Ω in the second, R3 = 150 Ω in the third and an unknown Rx in the fourth. At balance R2/R1 = Rx/R3, so Rx = R2R3/R1 = 200 × 150 / 100 = 300 Ω. In a Maxwell bridge with R2 = 1 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and C1 = 0.1 µF in parallel, L = R2R3C1 = 1000 × 10 000 × 0.1 × 10⁻⁶ = 1 H. Find Rx and L.
chapters.trap: Do not use the Wheatstone bridge for resistances below about 1 Ω, where lead and contact resistance swamp the answer; that is why the Kelvin double bridge with four terminals exists. Also match the bridge to the quantity: Maxwell and Hay for inductance, Schering for capacitance.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (inductive and capacitive transducers) for impedance ideas.
chapters.leave: Detailed phasor derivations and a.c. bridge screens; measurement of frequency and phase.

chapters.idea: Filters decide which frequencies reach the next stage, pre-amplifiers raise weak signals without much added noise, and differential and isolation amplifiers reject what both inputs share.
chapters.depth: Filter types: low pass, high pass, band pass, band stop and the narrow notch used to kill 50 Hz mains pickup. Cutoff at the −3 dB point, order, and roll-off of 20 dB per decade (6 dB per octave) per order. Passive RC and active Sallen-Key in outline. Pre-amplifier: low noise, high input impedance, gain, impedance matching to the source. Differential amplifier: differential gain Ad, common-mode gain Acm, CMRR = 20 log₁₀(Ad/Acm), resistor tolerance limiting real CMRR, the three op-amp instrumentation amplifier. Isolation amplifier: transformer or opto coupling, isolation voltage, breaking ground loops, patient safety. Mention surge protection at the input.

figure.aria: Two curves against normalised frequency: the low-pass gain falls from 1 while the high-pass gain rises to 1, both crossing 0.707 at f/fc equal to 1.

chapters.example: A first-order low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. fc = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 1000 × 10⁻⁷) = 1592 Hz. At 10 kHz the ratio f/fc = 6.28, so gain = 1/√(1 + 6.28²) = 0.157, which is 20 log₁₀ 0.157 = −16 dB. A differential amplifier has Ad = 1000 and Acm = 0.5, so CMRR = 20 log₁₀(1000/0.5) = 66 dB. Find fc, the gain at 10 kHz and the CMRR.
chapters.trap: The CMRR you calculate from resistor values is the ideal figure; with 1% resistors it collapses, and a small resistor mismatch can drop a designed 100 dB to about 60 dB. Also do not confuse the filter's cutoff with the amplifier's own bandwidth or slew-rate limit.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 (the conditioning chain) and basic op-amp circuits.
chapters.leave: Active filter design tables and op-amp internal design; bridge circuits to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Display instruments turn an electrical quantity into a number or a trace, trading accuracy, bandwidth and the ability to catch a one-time event.
chapters.depth: DVM: counts, so a 3½ digit meter has 2000 counts, resolution = range/counts, accuracy quoted as ±(% of reading + counts), ramp and integrating types, autozero. Multimeter: voltage, current, resistance, continuity, input impedance around 10 MΩ, burden voltage on current ranges. CRO block diagram: CRT with electron gun, vertical and horizontal deflection plates and phosphor screen; vertical attenuator and amplifier; time base and horizontal amplifier; trigger circuit; power supply. Electrostatic deflection and deflection sensitivity in volts per division, and the effect of the accelerating voltage. DSO: sampling rate, memory depth, pre-trigger, aliasing, single-shot capture. Spectrum analyser: swept superheterodyne with resolution bandwidth and span, noise floor, and the FFT analyser alternative.

figure.title: CRO block diagram
figure.aria: A CRO block diagram: the input goes through attenuator and vertical amplifier to the vertical plates, the triggered time base drives the horizontal amplifier and horizontal plates, and both plate pairs act on the CRT screen.

chapters.example: A 3½ digit DVM on the 2 V range has 2000 counts, so resolution = 2 V/2000 = 1 mV. Its accuracy is ±(0.5% of reading + 2 counts). Measuring 1.000 V gives ±(0.005 × 1.000 + 2 × 0.001) = ±0.007 V, that is ±7 mV. A DSO samples at 100 MS/s with a 1 µs/div time base over 10 divisions, so the record is 10 µs long and holds 100 × 10⁶ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 1000 samples. Find the DVM error and the DSO record length and sample count.
chapters.trap: A 3½ digit display has 2000 counts (1999 plus sign), not 3000, so resolution is range/2000. On a DSO, a sampling rate below twice the signal frequency folds the waveform to a false low frequency, and the trace looks stable while being wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.9 for amplifiers and filters ahead of the display.
chapters.leave: Digital display and LCD drive technology; sensor-side measurement to earlier units.
